scenario: AITA for telling my sister that her beating breast cancer was not impressive and not inspirational? | Three years ago my older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Within six months her cancer was cleared. She had minor radiAtion and then hormone therapy afterwards. She is 100% fine and healthy no need for surgery. We all came together and supported her during this time. Now, the thing has been is that she hasn’t stopped to remind us constantly about how she is a cancer survivor. And has made it her identity. She has since plastered it all over social media. I don’t mind it because I can choose to ignore it. But this holiday season she was insufferable. My breaking point happened when my dad who has been dealing with nerve problems was telling us how physical therapy wasn’t working for him and he will likely need to get surgery. My sister started bringing up her cancer story again. I snapped and told her that her surviving breast cancer was not impressive nor inspiration, it has a survival rate of 96% and to stop making everything about her story. My sister walked out of the room. I thought my family would back me up but instead my parents backed up my sister. My dad didn’t say anything but he was on my sisters side. I don’t know maybe what I said wasn’t the nicest way but I don’t think I was wrong in what I said.

The person who told her it wasn't impressive is her younger brother. He snapped at her during a family gathering when their dad was talking about his own health issues, and the sister brought up her cancer story again. The brother said that surviving breast cancer isn't impressive because the survival rate is 96%, and he told her to stop making everything about her story. The sister left the room, and the parents backed her up instead of the brother. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for the brother to say that? And why? I think I need to consider a few things here. First, the brother's perspective: he feels that his sister is constantly bringing up her cancer story, even when it's not relevant, like during their dad's health discussion. He might feel that she's using her experience to overshadow others or to gain attention. He also points out that breast cancer has a high survival rate, so maybe he thinks it's not as impressive as other cancers with lower survival rates. On the other hand, the sister's perspective: she went through a serious illness, and it's understandable that she would want to share her story, especially if it's something that has had a significant impact on her life. Cancer is a life-changing experience, and many people find strength and purpose in sharing their journeys. She might feel that her brother doesn't understand the emotional weight of her experience. Also, the parents' reaction is interesting. They backed up the sister, which might indicate that they see her experience as valid and important. Maybe they feel that the brother was too harsh in his words, even if he had some valid points. I also need to think about the context of the conversation. The brother snapped at his sister during a discussion about their dad's health issues. It might have been a tense moment, and the sister bringing up her cancer story could have been seen as insensitive or self-centered, especially if the family was focused on their dad's struggles. But then again, the sister might have been trying to offer support or relate to her dad's situation by sharing her own experience. It's possible that she didn't realize how it might have come across as self-centered. Another angle is the brother's choice of words. He told her that her survival wasn't impressive or inspirational because of the high survival rate. While it's true that breast cancer has a relatively high survival rate compared to other cancers, that doesn't diminish the individual's experience. Each person's journey with cancer is unique, and what might seem statistically common can still be incredibly challenging and life-altering for the individual. Moreover, telling someone that their experience isn't impressive or inspirational can be hurtful, especially if that person has been open about their struggles. It might make the sister feel invalidated or misunderstood, which could damage the sibling relationship. I also wonder about the brother's intentions. Was he trying to shut down the sister's constant reminders, or was he genuinely trying to address what he saw as an imbalance in how their family handles health issues? If he was trying to protect his dad from being overshadowed, that's one thing, but if he was just frustrated with his sister's behavior, that's another. In terms of whether it's right or wrong, I think it's more about the approach rather than the content of what he said. It's okay to have boundaries and to express when someone's behavior is affecting you, but the way he chose to do it might have been harsh or insensitive. Instead of directly calling her experience unimpressive, he could have expressed his feelings about how her constant reminders were affecting him and the family dynamic. Also, considering the high emotions involved, especially during a family gathering, it might have been better to address the issue privately rather than in front of everyone, which could have made the sister feel attacked or embarrassed. In conclusion, while the brother might have had valid frustrations with his sister's behavior, the way he expressed his feelings was likely hurtful and not the best approach. It's important to communicate concerns respectfully and considerately, especially when dealing with sensitive topics like health and family dynamics.
